newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.S. team to discuss press freedom in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. team to discuss press freedom in Cambodia.

text.p: Eight U.S. Congressmen, concerned about freedom of the press in Cambodia, flew into Phnom Penh on Monday to meet government officials and human rights leaders.
"We're very concerned about the human rights situation, we're very concerned about the freedom of the press here," House of Representatives delegation head John Porter told reporters on arrival.
"We believe that democracy cannot proceed without a free press and that will certainly be part of what we are looking into here," the Illinois Republican said.

On January 2, a young Cambodian newspaper editor was shot and wounded in an attack his colleagues suggested was politically motivated. Three local journalists have been murdered in the past two years.
Porter said the delegation would meet human rights leaders later on Monday.
They are scheduled to meet co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen during the three-day visit.
Human rights activists decry last year's perceived shift towards autocratic rule when relations grew frostier between the two premiers and their parties in the coalition government.
They forecast further deterioration in human rights as general elections, scheduled for 1998, near.

Porter said the U.S. team would visit the Tuol Sleng genocide museum, a former high school used by the Khmer Rouge to torture thousands of political prisoners during their 1975-79 Maoist rule which left more than one million people dead.
He said the delegation was keen to see progress in democratic principles launched with the U.N.-brokered peace accord of 1991.
The Khmer Rouge reneged on that pact, boycotted elections in 1993 and have fought the government since, although thousands of rebels have defected to the government in recent months.

Porter, a member of the house appropriations committee which handles foreign assistance, said the delegation wanted to "work with the government to protect the logging that is apparently destroying a great deal of the natural resources and environment of this country".

Cambodia last week declared a new ban on log exports a success but conceded the government did not have full control over the country's dwindling forests, especially in areas held by former Khmer Rouge guerrillas.
